title: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices

guide.summary: Unit 4 is taught in AP Precalculus but is not assessed on the AP Exam. It covers parametric functions and their rates of change, implicitly defined curves and conic sections, vectors and vector operations, matrices, inverses and determinants, linear transformations, and matrices as models of state transitions.

sections.heading: Parametric functions
sections.body: A parametric function gives x and y each as a function of a parameter t: (x(t), y(t)), tracing a curve with a direction of motion. Eliminating the parameter gives a rectangular equation, sometimes with a restricted domain. The average rate of change of x (or y) with respect to t is Δx/Δt; the slope of the curve between two parameter values is Δy/Δx. Circles and ellipses can be parametrized with x = h + a cos t, y = k + b sin t. Implicitly defined curves such as conics (circle, ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, hyperbola, parabola) relate x and y without solving for one.

sections.heading: Vectors
sections.body: A vector ⟨a, b⟩ has magnitude √(a² + b²) and direction angle θ with tan θ = b/a. Add vectors component-wise (tip-to-tail); scalar multiplication stretches or reverses. A unit vector has magnitude 1: v/|v|. Dot product: ⟨a, b⟩·⟨c, d⟩ = ac + bd = |u||v| cos θ; the dot product is zero for perpendicular vectors. Position and velocity of a moving particle can be modeled with vector-valued functions.

sections.heading: Matrices and transformations
sections.body: Matrix multiplication combines rows with columns; it is not commutative. For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc, and the inverse is (1/det)[[d, −b], [−c, a]], which exists only if det ≠ 0. A 2 × 2 matrix represents a linear transformation of the plane: rotation by θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]; |det| gives the area scale factor. Composition of transformations corresponds to matrix multiplication. Transition matrices model systems moving between states (Markov chains); multiplying the state vector by the matrix gives the next state, and repeated multiplication can approach a steady state.

sections.heading: Worked example: parametric motion
sections.body: A particle moves with x(t) = 2t and y(t) = t² − 4 for t ≥ 0. Eliminating the parameter gives t = x/2 and y = x²/4 − 4, a parabola, but only the right half is traced because x ≥ 0. At t = 1, the position is (2, −3), and the average rate of change of y with respect to x from t = 0 to t = 2 is (0 − (−4))/(4 − 0) = 1.

sections.heading: Worked example: vectors and matrices
sections.body: For u = ⟨3, 4⟩, the magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = 5 and a unit vector in the same direction is ⟨0.6, 0.8⟩. The dot product of u and v = ⟨4, −3⟩ is 12 − 12 = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular. A 2×2 matrix A = [[a, b], [c, d]] has determinant ad − bc; if the determinant is nonzero, A has an inverse, (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. A rotation matrix [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]] rotates vectors counterclockwise by θ, and the absolute value of the determinant gives the area scale factor of a linear transformation.

sections.heading: Exam note
sections.body: Remember that Unit 4 content is not assessed on the AP exam, but it supports later coursework in calculus and linear algebra.

sections.heading: Linear transformations
sections.body: Matrices represent linear transformations: multiplying a vector by a matrix maps it to a new vector. Composition of transformations corresponds to matrix multiplication, applied right to left. A transition matrix can model change between states, such as the proportion of customers switching between two companies each year, and repeated multiplication predicts long-run behavior.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: Even though Unit 4 isn't tested on the AP exam, practicing it builds skills for calculus courses that use parametric and vector functions.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know parameter, vector, magnitude, unit vector, dot product, determinant, inverse matrix, and transition matrix.

sections.heading: Practice habit
sections.body: Draw vectors and transformations on grid paper to check your algebraic results visually.

keyTakeaways: det = ad − bc; inverse requires det ≠ 0.
State vector × transition matrix = next state.
commonMistakes: Forgetting domain restrictions after eliminating a parameter.
Swapping the wrong entries in the 2 × 2 inverse.
examTips: This unit is not on the AP Exam but appears in course assessments.
Check transformation matrices on simple vectors like ⟨1, 0⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩.
For parametric questions, make a table of t, x, y values.
Verify an inverse by multiplying to get the identity.
guide.cramSheet:
**Parametric:** (x(t), y(t)) · slope Δy/Δx · ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t

**Vectors:** |v| = √(a² + b²) · unit v/|v| · u·v = ac + bd = |u||v| cos θ

**Matrices:** det = ad − bc · A⁻¹ = (1/det)[[d, −b], [−c, a]]

**Transformations:** rotation [[cos, −sin], [sin, cos]] · |det| = area factor

**Markov:** next state = M × state

vocab.definition: A function that defines x and y separately in terms of a parameter.
A relation between x and y not solved for either variable.
A curve such as a circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola.
A quantity with magnitude and direction.
A matrix A⁻¹ with AA⁻¹ = I.
A function on vectors represented by matrix multiplication.
A matrix giving probabilities of moving between states.
A state vector that remains unchanged under the transition matrix.

practice.topic: 4.11 The Inverse and Determinant of a Matrix
practice.frqType: Unit 4 Practice (not on the AP Exam)
practice.prompt: Let A = [[2, 3], [1, 4]] and v = ⟨1, 2⟩ (as a column vector).

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Find det(A) and explain what it tells you about how A transforms areas.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Find A⁻¹ and verify that A⁻¹(Av) = v.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Solve the system 2x + 3y = 13, x + 4y = 14 using A⁻¹.

rubric.description: A multiplies areas by 5 and preserves orientation (positive determinant); it is invertible.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Av = ⟨2(1) + 3(2), 1(1) + 4(2)⟩ = ⟨8, 9⟩.

B. det(A) = 2(4) − 3(1) = 5. The transformation multiplies the area of any region by 5, and because the determinant is positive it preserves orientation. Since det ≠ 0, A is invertible.

C. A⁻¹ = (1/5)[[4, −3], [−1, 2]]. A⁻¹⟨8, 9⟩ = (1/5)⟨32 − 27, −8 + 18⟩ = (1/5)⟨5, 10⟩ = ⟨1, 2⟩ = v.

D. The system is A⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨13, 14⟩, so ⟨x, y⟩ = A⁻¹⟨13, 14⟩ = (1/5)⟨52 − 42, −13 + 28⟩ = (1/5)⟨10, 15⟩ = ⟨2, 3⟩. So x = 2, y = 3.
